meta.titre: Ray diagrams: locating images in lenses and plane mirrors

sections.contenu_markdown: A jeweller in the Bafoussam market uses a small glass lens to inspect a ring: the lens shows the stone larger and upright. A photographer at a wedding in Buea focuses a camera so that a sharp, smaller, upside-down picture is formed on the film or sensor. Drawing ray diagrams is how physicists find where such images appear and what they look like. The GCE O/L regularly asks you to construct an image with two rays, to describe it, or to show how a plane mirror or a magnifying glass works.

items: Light travels in straight lines called rays, and a ray is drawn with an arrowhead showing its direction.
A convex (converging) lens is thicker in the middle and bends parallel rays towards a point.
The normal is the line at right angles to a surface at the point where a ray meets it.

sections.titre: Ray diagrams: rules for lenses and plane mirrors
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Key terms for a convex lens:** the *principal axis* is the line through the centre of the lens at right angles to its faces; the *optical centre* $O$ is the centre of the lens; the *principal focus* $F$ is the point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after passing through the lens; the *focal length* $f$ is the distance $OF$. A lens has a principal focus on each side.

**Construction rules.** To find the image of the top of an object, draw any two of these three rays from that point:

1. A ray **parallel to the principal axis** is refracted so that it passes through the principal focus $F$ on the other side.
2. A ray through the **optical centre** goes straight on without bending.
3. A ray that passes through the **principal focus** on the object side emerges **parallel** to the axis.

The image of the top point is where the two rays meet (real image, drawn with solid lines) or where they appear to come from when traced backwards (virtual image, drawn with dotted lines). The image of the bottom of an object standing on the axis is on the axis.

| Object position | Image |
|---|---|
| beyond $2F$ | between $F$ and $2F$, real, inverted, diminished |
| at $2F$ | at $2F$, real, inverted, same size |
| between $F$ and $2F$ | beyond $2F$, real, inverted, magnified |
| at $F$ | at infinity (parallel emergent rays) |
| between lens and $F$ | same side as object, virtual, upright, magnified |

A **diverging (concave) lens** always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image between the object and the lens.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When you must show how an eye sees the image of an object in a plane mirror.
variantes.contenu_markdown: From a point on the object draw two rays to the mirror. At each point where a ray strikes the mirror, draw the normal and a reflected ray so that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The reflected rays diverge: extend them **backwards** behind the mirror with dotted lines; they meet at the image. The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, it is the same size, upright, virtual and laterally inverted. Add an arrowhead on the reflected ray going towards the eye.

variantes.nom: Convex lens as a magnifying glass
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the object is placed between the lens and its principal focus.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use rays 1 and 2: the refracted rays diverge, so trace them backwards with dotted lines to find the virtual image. With $f = 6\ \mathrm{cm}$, an object $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ high at $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens gives a virtual image $12\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens on the same side as the object, upright and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ high. The eye looks through the lens towards the object to see this larger image.

sections.enonce_markdown: An object $1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ tall stands upright on the principal axis of a convex lens of focal length $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$, $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens. Describe how to find the image with a scale drawing (scale 1 cm to 1 cm), and state the position, size and nature of the image.

etapes.justification: Use a horizontal line for the principal axis, a vertical line for the lens and mark $F$ at $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ on both sides.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Draw the object as an upright arrow, $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ to the left of the lens and $1.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ high.

etapes.justification: A ray parallel to the axis is refracted through the principal focus on the far side.
etapes.resultat_markdown: From the top of the object, draw a horizontal ray to the lens, then a line from that point through $F$ on the right, extended beyond.

etapes.justification: A ray through the optical centre is not deviated.
etapes.resultat_markdown: From the top of the object draw a straight line through the centre of the lens and extend it to the right.

etapes.justification: The two refracted rays meet at the image of the top of the object.
etapes.resultat_markdown: They cross 12 cm to the right of the lens and 3.0 cm below the axis.

etapes.justification: The object is at $6\ \mathrm{cm}$, which is between $F$ ($4\ \mathrm{cm}$) and $2F$ ($8\ \mathrm{cm}$).
etapes.resultat_markdown: The image is real (rays actually meet), inverted, and magnified: $\dfrac{3.0}{1.5} = 2$ times as tall as the object, and it is beyond $2F$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The image is formed **12 cm** from the lens on the opposite side from the object; it is **real, inverted and magnified**, **3.0 cm** high. (Check: $1/4 = 1/6 + 1/12$.)

items.erreur_markdown: A student draws the ray parallel to the axis passing straight through the lens without bending, and then uses it to locate the image.
items.pourquoi_faux: A ray parallel to the principal axis is refracted by a convex lens and must pass through the principal focus.
items.correction_markdown: Bend the ray at the lens so that it passes through $F$ on the far side.

items.erreur_markdown: A student draws solid lines for the backward extensions of rays when finding a virtual image.
items.pourquoi_faux: Virtual images are formed by rays that only appear to come from the image, not by real rays, so they must be shown with dotted lines.
items.correction_markdown: Use solid lines for real rays and dotted lines for extensions behind the mirror or in front of the lens.

items.erreur_markdown: In a plane mirror diagram the student measures the angles of incidence and reflection from the surface of the mirror.
items.pourquoi_faux: The law of reflection uses angles measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.
items.correction_markdown: Draw the normal at the point of incidence and make the angle of reflection equal to the angle of incidence, measured from the normal.

items.erreur_markdown: A student states that the image formed by a plane mirror is real because we can see it.
items.pourquoi_faux: A real image can be caught on a screen. The image in a plane mirror is behind the mirror where no light actually reaches, so it is virtual.
items.correction_markdown: State that the image is virtual, upright, same size, as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.

items.erreur_markdown: A student places an object between a convex lens and its principal focus and draws an inverted real image.
items.pourquoi_faux: Inside the focal length the refracted rays diverge and cannot meet on the far side. The image is virtual and upright.
items.correction_markdown: Trace the diverging rays backwards with dotted lines to the virtual, upright, enlarged image on the object's side.

items.enonce_markdown: A convex lens has a focal length of $8.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. An object $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ tall is placed $24\ \mathrm{cm}$ in front of the lens. Describe how to find the image with two rays and state its position, size and nature.
items.solution_markdown:
Draw (1) a ray from the top of the object parallel to the axis, which is refracted through the principal focus ($8\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens on the far side), and (2) a ray from the top of the object through the optical centre, which goes straight on. The object is beyond $2F$ ($16\ \mathrm{cm}$).

The rays cross at a point 12 cm from the lens, 1.5 cm below the axis (found from the scale drawing, and checked by $1/v = 1/8 - 1/24$, which gives $v = 12\ \mathrm{cm}$).

**The image is real, inverted and diminished (1.5 cm tall), formed 12 cm from the lens, between F and 2F.**

items.enonce_markdown: A girl stands $1.5\ \mathrm{m}$ in front of a large plane mirror. (a) How far is her image behind the mirror? (b) How far is the image from the girl? (c) She walks $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ towards the mirror. How far is the image from her now? (d) State two other characteristics of the image.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front: **1.5 m**.

(b) Distance from girl to image $= 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0\ \mathrm{m}$. **3.0 m.**

(c) New distance to the mirror $= 1.5 - 0.50 = 1.0\ \mathrm{m}$, so the distance to the image is $2 \times 1.0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m}$. **2.0 m.**

(d) The image is virtual (it cannot be caught on a screen), upright, the same size as the object and laterally inverted (left and right appear exchanged).

items.enonce_markdown: A convex lens of focal length $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ is used as a magnifying glass to look at an insect $3.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ long, held $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the lens. (a) Explain how to construct the image with two rays. (b) Find the position and size of the image, and state its nature. (c) Why must the insect be closer to the lens than the principal focus?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) From the top of the insect draw (1) a ray parallel to the axis, refracted through the principal focus $F$ on the far side, and (2) a ray through the optical centre, straight on. These rays diverge on the far side, so extend both **backwards** with dotted lines. They meet on the insect's side of the lens.

(b) The dotted lines meet 15 cm from the lens, on the same side as the insect (scale drawing; check with $\dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{v}$ in the real-is-positive convention, giving $v = -15\ \mathrm{cm}$, the minus sign meaning virtual). The size is $3.0 \times \dfrac{15}{6} = 7.5\ \mathrm{mm}$. **The image is virtual, upright, magnified 2.5 times (7.5 mm long), 15 cm from the lens.**

(c) Inside $F$ the refracted rays are still diverging, so the eye sees them as coming from a larger virtual image. If the object were beyond $F$ the rays would converge and form a real, inverted image instead.

items_markdown: To locate an image use two rays: one parallel to the axis (refracted through $F$) and one through the optical centre (not deviated); the third ray passes through $F$ and emerges parallel.
Real images are formed where rays actually meet (solid lines); virtual images are found by tracing rays backwards (dotted lines).
A convex lens used as a magnifying glass needs the object between the lens and $F$: the image is virtual, upright and magnified.
A plane mirror forms an image that is virtual, upright, the same size, laterally inverted, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
Use arrowheads on all rays and measure reflection angles from the normal.
